sources.source: Nelson's eight rules (bibliographic fact, primary paper paywalled)

items.item: a named eight-rule superset of the WECO zone-and-trend tests exists, codified by Lloyd S. Nelson in 1984, cited here without a verbatim quote
Control limits and specification limits answer two genuinely independent questions about the same number; a process can pass one and fail the other in either direction.

at.step: Reveal: control limits vs. specification limits

items.item: A measurement inside its own process's control band but outside the customer's spec band is not a contradiction, and not a bug in either limit — it's the two questions disagreeing, which is exactly what each is built to be able to do.

at.step: Reveal: in control and out of spec, at once

items.item: Every extra rule added to a chart is, mechanically, one more independent chance for ordinary noise to trip something — there is no sensitivity gain available without some matching cost in false alarms, in principle, before any simulation confirms the size of it.

at.step: Predict: does adding more zone rules ever cost anything?

items.item: NIST's own cited 91.75 figure is not an abstract property of 'the WECO rules' as a monolith — it is specifically what you get from combining rules 1, 2 and 3, and the number moves again the moment a fourth rule joins.

at.step: Reveal: the measured price, matching NIST

items.item: A commonly cited false-alarm number is only as meaningful as the exact rule set it was measured under; reusing someone else's headline figure after changing which rules are active is a silent, easy mistake.

at.step: Reveal: the eighth rule's own, separate cost

items.item: Cp measures whether the process's spread fits inside the tolerance at all; Cpk additionally measures whether the process is sitting where it should inside that tolerance — two processes can share the first number and differ sharply on the second.

at.step: Reveal: Cp and Cpk, the centring trap

items.item: A high Cp paired with a low Cpk is diagnostic, not just descriptive: it tells an engineer to go look for a centring problem (a biased setpoint, a miscalibrated gauge) rather than a variability problem (worn tooling, inconsistent material).

at.step: Reveal: Cp and Cpk, the centring trap

items.item: A control chart that looks unstable is sometimes measuring two stable processes layered on top of each other; the fix is a missing column in the data model (which tool, which shift), not a smarter statistical rule.

at.step: Reveal: one chart, split by tool, becomes two

items.item: Stratification can only happen after the fact if the attribute to stratify by was captured at the time of measurement — a quality system that records thickness without recording which tool made it has already thrown away the ability to ever find this bug.

at.step: Reveal: one chart, split by tool, becomes two

items.item: A non-conformance record and a CAPA record are, structurally, just more facts that reference other facts by key — the quality discipline's own vocabulary (cause, action, owner, due date, verification) maps directly onto the same keyed-reference pattern used everywhere else in this course.

at.step: Reveal: non-conformances and CAPAs, keyed to context

items.item: A CAPA's 'verified' flag starting false is itself a data-quality discipline: the record exists the moment the problem is found, before anyone has checked whether the fix actually worked, so the two states can never be silently conflated.

at.step: Reveal: non-conformances and CAPAs, keyed to context

items.item: Turning off a chart's extra rules because they 'cry wolf' changes nothing about the one remaining rule's own, independent false-alarm rate — a common but confused response to alert fatigue that treats the whole chart as one dial rather than several independent ones.

at.step: Prove it
